strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging problem: adapting a pretrained text-to-video model for joint music and text conditioning without motion-capture supervision or full model training.

The proposed system is practical and parameter-efficient, combining zero-initialized audio cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, selective layer placement, and a staged noise schedule. Training reportedly requires only one A100 for roughly 20 hours.

The experiments include component ablations, comparisons with both an audio-video model and the Mochi backbone, held-out AIST music, prompt control, tempo changes, longer generation, and qualitative failure cases.

The generated frames generally exhibit strong appearance quality and prompt adherence, while the quantitative results suggest that adding music conditioning does not substantially degrade Mochi's video quality.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim is not convincingly validated. All reported scores come from VideoLLaMA 2, with no human evaluation, validation of the proposed evaluator against human judgments, established beat-alignment metric, or uncertainty estimates. Most concerningly, audio-blind Mochi receives a beat-alignment score of 8.34 versus 8.89 for MusicInfuser and 8.95 for ground truth, indicating that the metric may largely reward plausible dancing rather than actual audio-motion correspondence. Shuffled-audio or temporally shifted-audio controls are also absent.

Baseline coverage and comparability are weak. MM-Diffusion is an older joint audio-video generator with different duration and capabilities—the paper even stretches its spectrogram—while Mochi cannot consume audio. There is no comparison with competitive music-conditioned motion/dance approaches followed by rendering, or stronger contemporary audio-conditioned human-generation systems. Consequently, the claimed superiority over prior work is insufficiently established.

Several headline generalization claims rely on very limited qualitative evidence: group choreography, doubled duration, unseen 'K-pop' music, difficulty control, and diversity are illustrated with a few examples but lack systematic measurement. Different random seeds alone also do not demonstrate absence of training-data memorization.

The individual technical ingredients have modest originality and incomplete justification. Zero-initialized cross-attention and LoRA are established techniques; the rank-64 argument based on homography degrees of freedom is not technically persuasive and is unsupported by a rank sweep. Layer selection optimizes an image-quality proxy rather than audio responsiveness, and the Beta-Uniform schedule yields mixed ablation results, improving the aggregate score only slightly while actually reducing reported style and beat alignment.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits important details including video resolution and frame count, batch size and optimizer settings, parameter counts, exact audio-video temporal alignment and feature shapes, the precise beta-decay schedule and its mapping to Mochi's noise parameterization, and clear definitions of ablation settings. The 15,799 YouTube clips also lack source lists, collection/filtering procedures, and licensing information. These are material issues for reproducing the reported model rather than presentation refinements.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging problem: adapting a strong text-to-video model to jointly follow music and text without requiring motion-capture supervision.

The proposed system is computationally practical: it freezes most of Mochi, adds audio cross-attention and rank-64 LoRA modules, and reports training in roughly 20 hours on one A100. The use of both AIST videos and in-the-wild dance videos is sensible for retaining visual diversity.

The manuscript includes component ablations, failure cases, held-out AIST music tracks, prompt-controlled examples, tempo perturbations, longer generation, and qualitative comparisons. The reported results suggest that audio conditioning can be added without substantially degrading the base model's visual or prompt-following capabilities.

The presentation is generally organized, and the supplementary material supplies evaluation prompts, test music identifiers, qualitative ablations, and limitations such as failures on faces, fingers, and overlapping silhouettes.
weaknesses: The central claim—meaningful synchronization of choreography to music—is not convincingly validated. Beat and style alignment are judged only by VideoLLaMA 2 using single 0–10 prompts. There is no validation of these scores against human judgments, no standard motion/music alignment measure, no beat-detection analysis, and no uncertainty or significance reporting. This is material because most reported differences are small; for example, beat alignment is 8.89 versus 8.56 for MM-Diffusion, while several ablations differ by only about 0.1–0.2.

The evaluation protocol risks circular or unreliable conclusions. The same unvalidated Video-LLM supplies all dance, video, prompt, and ablation scores, with unusually high scores even for competing systems. Although 100 videos per configuration are mentioned, the paper does not report score distributions, repeated evaluator runs, aggregation details, or sensitivity to prompts. No human study is provided for inherently subjective properties such as movement realism, creativity, style, and choreography complexity.

The baseline evidence is too weak for the breadth of the superiority claims. The quantitative comparison contains only an older joint audio-video model, MM-Diffusion, and the audio-unconditioned Mochi base model; these do not isolate the benefit of the proposed conditioning design against competitive audio-conditioned adaptation alternatives. MM-Diffusion also generates shorter videos in the displayed comparison, further complicating fairness. Comparisons to established music-to-dance methods are absent even on synchronization-related measures.

Several proposed components have limited originality or insufficient technical justification. ZICA is standard residual cross-attention with a zero-initialized output projection, and HR-LoRA is principally LoRA with rank 64. The argument that video requires higher rank because a homography has eight degrees of freedom does not establish an appropriate LoRA rank for transformer video adaptation. The 'No Higher Rank' setting is not defined, and no rank sweep, parameter-matched baseline, or cost analysis supports rank 64.

The Beta-Uniform schedule is underspecified and its rationale is not adequately established. The paper defines a Beta distribution on [0,1] but does not state precisely how samples map to Mochi's noise/timestep parameterization. Claims that low noise first learns task-specific fine motion while preserving coarse motion are asserted rather than demonstrated. In Table 4, removing this schedule actually improves style and beat alignment, while the claimed benefit rests mainly on body representation under the same unvalidated evaluator.

The layer-selection method does not directly measure 'adaptability' to audio. It selects the 16 of 48 layers with the best VBench imaging quality under STG perturbations of the base model. Why this criterion identifies layers suitable for audio cross-attention is unclear, exact selected indices are not provided, and the ablation compares only against applying ZICA without selection rather than random selections, evenly spaced layers, or parameter-matched alternatives.

The claimed generalization is not established by the presented experiments. SUNO-generated K-pop is called unseen because K-pop is absent from AIST, but the model also trains on 15,799 insufficiently characterized YouTube clips, so overlap in music or dance style cannot be excluded. Longer generation, group choreography, prompt-based difficulty control, and diversity are supported only by a few selected frame strips without quantitative or systematic testing. The tempo experiment also changes pitch, confounding tempo responsiveness with tonal changes.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the high-level implementation summary. Missing details include batch size, resolution and frame rate, optimizer settings, audio/video temporal alignment, projector architecture, LoRA target matrices, lower-rank baseline value, trainable parameter counts, precise schedule-to-noise mapping, exact layer indices, inference length/settings, and construction and licensing of the YouTube dataset. These omissions would make faithful reproduction difficult.

Overall, the adaptation idea is plausible and potentially useful, but the paper's main scientific evidence depends almost entirely on an unvalidated automatic judge and selected qualitative examples. This evidentiary gap, together with weak baseline coverage and under-justified technical novelty, outweighs the demonstrated merits in the current manuscript.

strengths: Addresses a useful and challenging problem: adapting a strong text-to-video model to music-conditioned dance generation while retaining prompt control, without requiring motion-capture supervision.

The lightweight design is practical: zero-initialized audio cross-attention and LoRA adapt Mochi in roughly 20 hours on one A100, making the approach potentially useful to other pretrained video models.
The manuscript is clear and visually polished. Figures 1, 5, and 11 show appealing frames, and the architecture and training recipe are explained at a high level.
The experiments cover several relevant capabilities, including unseen music, doubled sequence length, tempo changes, prompt-controlled scenes, group dancing, and output diversity.

The component ablations are reasonably broad. Table 4 compares layer selection, LoRA rank, LoRA removal, Beta-Uniform scheduling, and naive feature addition; the full system obtains the highest reported aggregate score.
The paper acknowledges inherited anatomical failures and includes concrete failure cases rather than presenting only successful generations.
weaknesses: The central synchronization claim is not adequately validated. Beat and style alignment are judged only by VideoLLaMA 2 using single-number prompts, with no human study, established beat-alignment measure, motion/beat analysis, or validation that these LLM scores correlate with human judgments. Static figures cannot independently demonstrate temporal synchronization.

The quantitative evidence is statistically weak. Although the supplement indicates 100 generated videos per configuration, the paper reports only means, without repeated runs, confidence intervals, variance, significance tests, or judge-sensitivity analysis. Several aggregate improvements are small—for example, 8.33 versus 8.22 in Table 4 and 8.96 versus 8.86 in prompt alignment—so their reliability is unclear.

Baseline coverage is limited and partly mismatched. MM-Diffusion is an older joint audio-video generator with substantially different capabilities, while Mochi receives no audio and therefore cannot test music synchronization. Comparisons to stronger contemporary human-animation, audio-driven video, or music-to-motion-plus-rendering pipelines are absent.

The claimed methodological novelty is moderate. Zero-initialized conditioning and LoRA adaptation are established techniques, while the justification for HR-LoRA is speculative: the homography degree-of-freedom argument does not establish that rank 64 is appropriate for dance video, and the ablation does not report the lower rank or provide a rank sweep.

Important technical and reproducibility details are missing, including video resolution, frame count and rate, audio-token temporal alignment, projector and cross-attention dimensions, exact selected layer indices, the Beta decay schedule, the mapping from the Beta variable to Mochi's noise parameterization, and key sampling settings. The statement that low noise corresponds to learning high-frequency details does not by itself justify the proposed curriculum.

The in-the-wild YouTube data are insufficiently documented: collection criteria, clip preprocessing, licensing, deduplication, and checks for overlap with evaluation music/content are not described. This limits reproducibility and leaves potential leakage and data-governance concerns.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. Unseen SUNO “K-pop” and three TikTok examples provide demonstrations rather than systematic generalization tests, and changing audio speed alters both tempo and pitch, so Figure 6 does not isolate responsiveness to tempo. Overall, the idea and qualitative results are promising, but the evaluation gaps keep the recommendation near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging problem: adding music responsiveness to a pretrained text-to-video model while retaining prompt-based control and avoiding intermediate skeletal motion representations.

The proposed system is practical and reasonably coherent. Selective zero-initialized cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, mixed controlled/in-the-wild training data, and the Beta-to-uniform noise schedule form a plausible low-cost adaptation pipeline. The reported training cost—4,000 steps in roughly 20 hours on one A100—is attractive.

The manuscript includes several relevant ablations. It compares the proposed layer selection with first, middle, last, evenly distributed, and all-layer alternatives, and separately examines zero initialization, LoRA rank, the noise schedule, in-the-wild data, and simple feature addition.

The qualitative examples cover diverse prompts, multiple dancers, non-human subjects, tempo changes, unseen synthetic music, longer generation, and failure cases. The authors also provide evaluation prompts, test-track identifiers, dataset sizes, and a 33-participant human study.

The results suggest a useful capability: MusicInfuser improves the reported dance-quality average over Mochi and MM-Diffusion while largely retaining Mochi's video and prompt quality. Acceptance does not require state-of-the-art benchmark performance, and the basic application and efficiency contribution have merit.
weaknesses: Material weakness: the central claim of music synchronization is not established with sufficiently objective evidence. Beat and style alignment are scored primarily by Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2, without established motion–beat metrics, beat-event analysis, temporal correspondence measurements, or uncertainty estimates. The very high and often saturated LLM scores in Table 1 further make small differences difficult to interpret.

Material weakness: the claimed validation of the Video-LLM metric is incomplete. The paper says it correlates well with human judgment, but reports no correlation coefficient or per-video paired analysis. Figure 9 only gives aggregate A/B preferences from 33 participants, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, number of judgments per condition, tie policy, or inter-rater agreement.

Material weakness: the baseline evidence is limited and partly mismatched. Mochi has no audio input, so outperforming it on music alignment is expected, while MM-Diffusion is an older joint audio-video model without equivalent text control. The paper provides no strong audio-conditioned video baseline with comparable pretrained visual capacity, and the EDGE comparison is described as qualitative rather than quantitatively evaluated. This prevents isolating how much benefit comes from the proposed adaptation method rather than the much stronger base generator.

Material weakness: the empirical support for the novel layer-adaptability criterion is weaker than the claims suggest. It adapts skip-guidance analysis from prior work and selects layers using pretrained-model imaging quality rather than music responsiveness. Improvements over simple layer choices are small under VideoLLaMA 2 (Table 5), no variability or significance is reported, and it is not shown that the criterion transfers across base models, datasets, adapter budgets, or random seeds.

The generalization claims rely mainly on selected qualitative examples. Nine-second outputs, SUNO-generated K-pop tracks, animals, and group dances are not evaluated systematically, and varying a seed does not by itself rule out memorization. There is also no quantitative temporal-consistency analysis for generation beyond the approximately 2.5-second training clips.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper does not clearly specify the selected layer indices in accessible form, the fraction of captions replaced by base prompts, video resolution and frame rate, inference sampling settings, detailed audio-projector architecture and temporal alignment procedure, or sufficiently precise collection and preprocessing information for the 15,799 YouTube clips. No code or trained-model release is identified.

The technical novelty is moderate: zero-initialized conditioning, LoRA, cross-attention, and skip-guidance are established components, while the Beta-to-uniform schedule is straightforward. Their combination is sensible, but the current evidence does not convincingly demonstrate that the proposed layer criterion and schedule are broadly reliable advances rather than task-specific engineering choices.

Presentation refinements include several overstatements such as “significantly outperforms” without statistical testing and claims that selected visual examples “show” strong generalization. These could be corrected editorially, but the missing objective synchronization evaluation, adequately matched baselines, and statistical analysis are consequential and currently make the balance favor rejection.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant and difficult problem: generating visually realistic dance directly from music and text without requiring an intermediate skeleton or motion-capture representation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/e96bd8b1cd4147a7af58a129c3166924/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed adaptation recipe is practical: zero-initialized audio cross-attention, LoRA, selective layer insertion, and a noise-level curriculum preserve a strong pretrained video prior while reportedly allowing training on one A100 in about 20 hours.

The qualitative examples suggest reasonably strong appearance, prompt adherence, and subject/scene diversity. The paper also discusses inherited failures involving faces, hands, silhouettes, and fast motion.

The authors include component and layer-selection ablations evaluated by two video-language models, as well as a 33-participant human comparison. This is more diagnostic effort than presenting only cherry-picked generation examples.
weaknesses: The central music-synchronization claim is not supported by sufficiently reliable measurement. Beat and style alignment are judged mainly by VideoLLaMA 2 and Qwen3-Omni using single 0–10 prompts. There is no established beat/onset alignment metric, motion-beat analysis, calibration study, repeated-query variance, or statistical uncertainty. The claimed correlation with human judgment is not actually reported: Figure 9 gives pairwise preferences against MM-Diffusion, but no sample-level correlation coefficient or agreement analysis between humans and the proposed automatic scores.

The baseline evidence is too weak to establish the paper's broad superiority claims. The main quantitative comparison uses the old, generic MM-Diffusion and the audio-unconditioned Mochi backbone; these differ substantially in modality, capacity, output quality, and likely resolution. The human study compares only against MM-Diffusion. Although the text states that EDGE is compared in the main paper, no controlled quantitative EDGE comparison is presented. Consequently, the results do not isolate progress in music-conditioned dance generation from the benefit of starting with a much stronger video generator.

The automatic evaluation exhibits warning signs that are not examined. Many scores saturate near 9–10, Qwen assigns the generated method perfect body representation despite acknowledged anatomical failures, and generated videos exceed ground truth on some subjective dimensions. Showing that ground truth is higher on only selected metrics is not adequate validation of the proposed evaluator.

The proposed layer-adaptability criterion has limited conceptual and empirical support. It ranks layers by VBench imaging quality under skip guidance, which does not directly measure how suitable a layer is for audio conditioning. The resulting improvements over simple layer placements are modest—for example, 8.14 versus 7.99 overall with Qwen and 8.33 versus 8.15 with VideoLLaMA—and no multiple-seed variation or significance analysis is provided. Details of the samples, seeds, and guidance settings used to compute the ranking are also absent.

Several method components are combinations or minor adaptations of established techniques: zero-initialized conditioning, cross-attention adapters, LoRA, and curriculum-like noise sampling. The paper does not convincingly demonstrate that the Beta-Uniform schedule or layer selection yields a substantial advance; their overall-score gains are small, and there are no direct measurements of the claimed savings in trainable parameters, memory, FLOPs, or training time relative to all-layer adaptation.

Claims of generalization to unseen genres, unconventional subjects, longer videos, and speed control are predominantly qualitative. A few SUNO-generated K-pop examples, animal frames, and sequences up to nine seconds do not establish systematic out-of-distribution or long-horizon performance. Likewise, varying a few random seeds does not substantiate the claim that the model has not memorized dance routines.

The human-study protocol is materially underspecified. The manuscript gives 33 participants and four forced-choice questions, but not the number of evaluated pairs, participant workload, assignment scheme, presentation randomization details, exclusions, confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-rater reliability. The very large preference margins therefore cannot be properly interpreted.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation and data details: the exact selected layer indices, Beta decay schedule, mapping from the Beta variable to diffusion noise scale, LoRA target modules, ZICA placement and dimensions, audio/video temporal alignment, resolution, frame rate, sampling settings, and inference cost are not fully reported. The 15,799 YouTube clips are described only as coming from four playlists, without sufficient identifiers or a reproducible collection/filtering protocol. No concrete code, model, or evaluation release statement is provided.

There are also presentation issues—overstated uses of “significantly,” some grammatical errors, and conclusions drawn from static frame strips that cannot demonstrate synchronization—but these are secondary. The determining concerns are the unvalidated evaluation, weak and mismatched comparisons, and insufficient quantitative support for the main synchronization and generalization claims. The idea is worthwhile, so this is a weak reject rather than a clear reject.

strengths: The paper addresses a compelling and useful problem: adapting a pretrained text-to-video model to jointly follow music and text while avoiding motion-capture or reconstructed-pose supervision.

MusicInfuser is technically sensible and resource-conscious. The combination of zero-initialized audio cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, a noise-level curriculum, and selective placement in 16 of 48 DiT layers preserves the strong Mochi prior while enabling audio conditioning; training reportedly takes about 20 hours on one A100.

The layer-adaptability criterion is an interesting contribution. Selecting layers through their constructive influence during guided sampling is more principled than simply choosing early, middle, late, or uniformly spaced layers, and it avoids combinatorial fine-tuning searches.

The evaluation includes component ablations, two Video-LLM evaluators, 100 samples per model configuration, and a 33-participant human study. Both automatic evaluations favor the proposed layer selection, and the human comparison reports large preferences over MM-Diffusion in quality, alignment, realism, and complexity.

The method demonstrates useful flexibility, including prompt-controlled appearance and setting, multiple subjects, tempo responsiveness, unseen music, diverse generations from different seeds, and sequences up to nine seconds. The qualitative results generally show good visual consistency and prompt adherence.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, and it candidly documents inherited failures involving faces, fingers, fast motion, and ambiguous silhouettes.
weaknesses: The evidence for the central synchronization claim is weaker than it should be. Beat and style alignment are judged primarily by general-purpose Video-LLMs, without established signal- or pose-based synchronization measures such as beat-alignment error, motion-beat correlation, or tempo-response statistics. The tempo and long-video results are qualitative.

The claimed validation of the Video-LLM metric is incomplete. Figure 9 shows that humans and the metric favor the same method, but no sample-level correlation coefficient, confidence interval, significance test, or comparison against established metrics is reported. Several scores are also near the ceiling, limiting discrimination.

The human evaluation lacks important statistical details: the number of comparisons contributed by each participant, assignment and randomization procedure, treatment of ties, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, and significance tests are not given. It compares only against MM-Diffusion, not Mochi or the principal ablations.

Baseline coverage is limited. MM-Diffusion is an older general audio-video model, while Mochi has no audio input, so neither is a particularly strong matched competitor for music-conditioned dance video generation. Skeleton-based EDGE is discussed largely qualitatively, and relevant contemporary human-animation or audio-conditioned video approaches are not empirically compared.

The novelty of several components individually is modest: zero-initialized cross-attention, LoRA, and curriculum noise sampling are adaptations of familiar techniques. The layer-selection criterion is the most distinctive element, but its rationale remains heuristic, and the paper does not test whether selected layers transfer across base models, datasets, metrics, or adaptation budgets.

Efficiency claims are insufficiently quantified. Reporting one A100 and roughly 20 training hours is useful, but there is no comparison of trainable parameters, memory, throughput, or training cost against adapting all layers or other conditioning strategies. The phrase 'except for experiments requiring more capacity' is also ambiguous.

Reproduction would require additional details, including selected layer indices, exact Beta-Uniform decay and mapping to the model's noise range, ZICA and LoRA placement, audio-video temporal alignment, projector/downsampling architecture, frame rate, resolution, inference settings, optimizer configuration, and precise collection/filtering information for the 15,799 YouTube clips. No code or model-release statement is provided.

The in-the-wild data provenance raises reproducibility and possible licensing concerns. The paper names four YouTube playlists but does not identify them or explain deduplication, filtering, synchronization quality, or checks for overlap with evaluation content.
